name: Potentino Castle
region: Tuscany — Seggiano, Grosseto Province, Monte Amiata, Maremma
architectural_style: Medieval origin, under the Bishop of Chiusi for nearly two centuries; later held by several noble Sienese families; restored since 2000 by the Greene family after near-total ruin

tagline: Rebuilt from near-total ruin since 2000, on an isolated Amiata hillside once held by the Bishop of Chiusi
highlights: Restored since 2000 by the Greene family, starting from a state of near-total ruin
Nearly a thousand years overlooking the isolated Amiata valley
Functions as a permanent cultural laboratory alongside its wine, oil and spirits estate
description:
For nearly two centuries, Potentino Castle was under the control of the Bishop of Chiusi, until the arrival of Sienese forces brought it under their own control, after which it passed through various noble Sienese families — the Bonsignori, Tolomei, Salimbeni, Bindi, Venturini and Venturi — over the following centuries. Its position in the isolated Amiata valley, beyond the Vivo stream, in the northern part of Seggiano's municipal territory, kept it relatively removed from Tuscany's major historical routes and conflicts.

When the Greene family acquired the castle in 2000, it was little more than a ruin: collapsed roofs, spaces overtaken by vegetation, no working utilities, and rooms filled with rubble. After a comprehensive restoration, the castle today combines accommodation with a working agricultural estate producing wine, extra virgin olive oil, and quality spirits, alongside functioning as a permanent cultural laboratory.

The near-total ruin the Greene family found in 2000 makes Potentino's restoration one of the more dramatic recovery stories in this collection, closer to genuine reconstruction from rubble than the more common pattern of gradual renovation of a still-standing building.

The castle's isolated position in the Amiata valley, away from Tuscany's major medieval trade and conflict routes, likely contributed to both its long survival and its relative historical obscurity compared to the more strategically contested castles of the Chianti or Val d'Orcia.

The estate's identity as a "permanent cultural laboratory," alongside its wine and spirits production, gives Potentino an active programming dimension distinct from castles that function purely as static heritage accommodation.

Monte Amiata's hiking and nature trails, along with the nearby Brunello wine route around Montalcino, give guests staying at Potentino a genuine mix of outdoor activity and wine tourism within a short drive.

By 2000, when the Greene family acquired it, the castle was nearly a total ruin. After a comprehensive restoration, it today combines accommodation with a working estate producing wine, olive oil, and spirits, and functions as a permanent cultural laboratory on an isolated hillside of Monte Amiata.

faqs.question: Was Potentino Castle really in ruins before its restoration?
faqs.answer: Yes — when the Greene family acquired it in 2000, the castle had collapsed roofs, no working utilities, and rooms filled with rubble and vegetation.

faqs.question: Are all the rooms at Potentino Castle within the historic building?
faqs.answer: Yes — the 10 rooms and 2 apartments are all within the same restored historic structure, with no separate modern annex identified.

faqs.question: What is Potentino's "cultural laboratory"?
faqs.answer: An ongoing program of cultural events held at the estate alongside its wine, olive oil and spirits production — worth checking the calendar if you want to combine your stay with an event.

hotel.how_to_stay:
**Getting there:** About 20 minutes from Seggiano and 1 hour from Grosseto by car; the closest airport is Rome-Fiumicino (~2h) or Florence-Peretola (~1h45). A very rural area — a car is essential.

**Rooms & rates:** 10 rooms within the main castle (capacity up to 20 people) and 2 apartments (2-8 people), with period furnishings, some with exposed wooden beams and others with frescoed ceilings. From €180/night.

**On-site:** Own winery (wine, oil, spirits), cultural events, gardens.

**Good to know:** It's also a "permanent cultural laboratory" with periodic events — worth checking the calendar if you want to combine your stay with a cultural activity.

**Combine with:** Monte Amiata (hiking and nature), Seggiano (~20 min), Montalcino and its Brunello wine route (~45 min), the thermal springs at Saturnia (~50 min).
